sections.body:
A request for a raise is a business case with a person attached. You are asking an organisation that has a budget to move money from one place to another, and you are the one who has to explain why that move is the right decision. Everything else is packaging.

This sounds cold, and it is not. It is the opposite of cold. A request presented as a favour ("I was hoping you might consider...") puts the manager in an awkward position, because they cannot say yes to a favour without a reason and cannot say no to a favour without looking unkind. A request presented as a case gives them something they can take to their own manager, which is usually what they need to do.

Three things make a pay case work, and all three have to be there.

First, **evidence of your contribution**. Not a feeling that you have worked hard, but a record of what you did and what it was worth: a project you delivered, a cost you cut, a process you fixed, a customer you kept. Money is the strongest evidence, but not the only kind.

Second, **a market figure**. What the same role costs elsewhere, for someone with your experience, in your city or your market. This turns your request from a personal wish into a market observation.

Third, **a specific number and a specific form**. "I would like to discuss my salary" is not a request. "I would like my salary to move from $1,500 to $1,800 per month" is. Whether the answer is a percentage, a monthly figure or an annual figure, say which one you mean, and say it out loud without apologising.

Two things are worth saying plainly. First, a raise is not the only way to be paid better: a bonus, extra leave, a training budget or a title change are all real outcomes, and in some companies the pay scale is fixed, which means only a change of band or role can move it. Second, you cannot control your manager's answer, but you can control the quality of your case, and that is worth something on its own, because it is the same material you will use at the next review.
examples: I would like to talk about my salary, and I have put together some figures.
My salary is $1,500 a month, and I am asking for $1,800.
The role pays $1,700 to $1,900 in comparable companies, and my current rate is below that band.
I would like my salary to move from $1,500 to $1,800 per month.
sections.heading: What asking for a raise actually is

sections.body:
An unasked question is a wish. A prepared question is a request. Put two hours into the preparation and the conversation itself takes five minutes.

Start with a written list of the last twelve months. Not a memory, a list. Write down what you delivered, with a number attached to each item where one exists. This is the part people skip, and it is the part that makes the difference between a request and a complaint.

Then find the market figure. Look at job advertisements for the same role in the same city, at two or three levels: entry, your level, and one step above. Salaries are published in more places than people think, and your own network is better data than any website, because people will tell you their actual number.

Then decide what you are asking for, and write it as one sentence with a number. Ask for slightly more than you would settle for. If you want $1,800, say $1,850, because there is almost always a step down in the conversation and it is easier for the other side to move towards you than for you to move down.

Then write the opening sentence and say it out loud. Not in your head, out loud, five times. People who have said the sentence once in a real conversation handle the answer far better.

Finally, decide your fallback. If the answer is no, what is your next move: a review date, a bonus instead, a title change, more responsibility? Having a second option means you can respond calmly instead of ending the conversation in a dead end.
examples: Ask for $1,850, because I would settle for $1,800.
My three strongest points are the delivery cut, the churn figure and the new client.
If the answer is no, I will ask for a review date in six months and a bonus this quarter.
sections.heading: How to prepare before you ask
steps: Write down what you delivered in the last twelve months, with numbers.
Find market figures for your role and level in your city.
Decide one specific number to ask for and write it as a sentence.
Practise the opening sentence out loud, five times.
Decide your fallback before the conversation, not during it.

sections.body:
Timing matters as much as the case. The best moment is rarely the day something goes wrong, and never the day you are angry.

Good moments. After a project you delivered well, particularly if the result is known and the praise is recent. After you take on a role that is clearly bigger than your current title. After a strong performance review. After you have taken on responsibilities that nobody formally gave you and you have been doing them for months. Before a budget cycle closes, because budgets that are not claimed by a deadline are lost.

Bad moments. When you are tired, rushed or upset. When the company is announcing layoffs or a bad quarter. When your manager is on leave. Immediately after a colleague has left under difficult circumstances. When the news is that you were praised in a way that clearly came with a lower rating.

The setting matters just as much. **Ask in a private, scheduled meeting**, ideally a one-to-one, and ideally booked with a stated purpose. "Could I book twenty minutes with you on Thursday to talk about my pay?" is better than springing it in a corridor, because it gives the manager time to prepare, and it avoids a conversation that gets cut short.

Some managers prefer email. If you ask by email, ask for the meeting rather than making the case in the email. A short email, one or two lines, that ends with a request for time is enough.

One more thing to check before you choose the moment: **does your company have a pay review cycle?** Many large employers review salaries on fixed dates, sometimes once a year, and some will not move a salary outside that cycle at all. Asking at the wrong time does not make you rude, but it makes you uninformed. If you do not know, ask your manager directly: "Is there a set time of year when salaries are reviewed?"

And if you have just started the job, wait. Six to twelve months of visible contribution is the minimum that makes a request reasonable, whatever your contract says.
examples: Could I book twenty minutes with you on Thursday to talk about my pay?
Is there a set time of year when salaries are reviewed?
I would rather raise this in a proper conversation than in the corridor.
I have been covering the finance reporting since March, which is why I am asking now.
sections.heading: Choosing the moment and the setting

sections.body:
The strongest pay case is short. One page, or one sheet of paper, and it can be read in three minutes. If it cannot, it will not be read.

Put the numbers first. A simple structure works: what you do now, what that was worth, and what the market pays. For example.

"I am currently responsible for the whole monthly reporting cycle, which used to take three days and now takes four hours. I also took over the customer onboarding process in March. My salary is $1,500 a month. The same role in comparable companies pays $1,700 to $1,900." That is a complete case, in three sentences.

Three kinds of evidence work, and they are strongest when combined.

Results. Money saved, revenue gained, time reduced, errors fixed, customers retained, projects delivered on time. "I reduced the monthly reporting time from three days to four hours" is worth roughly $4,000 a year in staff time, and you can say so.

Scope. New responsibilities, a bigger team, a second market, a system you now own. "I took over customer onboarding in March, which previously sat with another team." This is the part most people forget, and it is often the strongest, because it describes what you will be paid for in future, not only what you have already delivered.

Market. The published range for your role and level, in your city. Name the source if it is a real one: "The range advertised for this role in Hanoi is $1,700 to $1,900." If you only have one data point, say so honestly: "Two people I know in similar roles are on about $1,800."

Watch out for two mistakes. **Do not compare yourself to a colleague**, especially not one who negotiates better; it turns a business case into a complaint about fairness. **Do not stack every good thing you have ever done.** Pick the three strongest and let them stand. A long list reads as pride rather than evidence.

And if you do not have good numbers yet, say so honestly and use scope instead: "My results this year have been hard to measure, but my remit has grown from one customer to nine." Managers can work with that. They cannot work with a feeling.
examples: I reduced the monthly reporting time from three days to four hours, which is about $4,000 a year in staff time.
I took over customer onboarding in March, which previously sat with another team.
The range advertised for this role is $1,700 to $1,900.
I am not asking to be paid more for the same job. I am asking for the job I am now doing.
sections.heading: Building the case with numbers

sections.body:
You will only get one natural opening, so spend it on your best sentence. Prepare that sentence and keep everything else flexible.

A good opening has four moves: thank, evidence, request, pause. Something like this.

"Thank you for making the time. I want to talk about my pay, because my responsibilities have changed since I started in this role. I have taken over the monthly reporting and the onboarding process, and I have cut the reporting time from three days to four hours. My salary is $1,500 a month, and I would like to ask for $1,800."

Then **stop talking**. This is the part people get wrong. After the number, most candidates keep talking, because silence feels like failure. It is not. The silence is where the manager thinks, and the more you fill it, the less they listen to.

Three things not to say. **Do not apologise for asking.** "I know this is a difficult time" is fine once, as context. "I am sorry to ask" is not; it undercuts your own case before it starts. **Do not compare yourself to others**, especially not to a colleague's salary. **Do not make it a verdict.** "I deserve more" asks the manager to argue a moral case; "the role has changed and the market rate is $1,700 to $1,900" asks them to make a decision they can defend.

And be ready for a second sentence, because the most common reply is a question: "Tell me about the reporting work." That is interest, not rejection. Answer it in one minute and then return to your request: "Is $1,800 something we could look at?"

If the manager says they need to think about it, that is a normal answer. Say: "Of course. What would you need from me to help you decide?" This turns a vague delay into a specific next step, and it shows that you are organised about the process.
examples: Thank you for making the time. I want to talk about my pay, because my responsibilities have changed since I started.
My salary is $1,500 a month, and I would like to ask for $1,800.
Is $1,800 something we could look at?
Of course. What would you need from me to help you decide?
sections.heading: How to say it out loud

sections.body:
Three answers are possible, and each has a correct response. Most people only prepare for one of them.

Yes. Do not gush, and do not immediately accept without checking what you are agreeing to. Say: "Thank you, I appreciate that. Can I see the revised figure in writing, and when does it start?" Then confirm the start date, the new figure, and whether it is written into your contract or a letter. A verbal yes that never appears in writing is worth very little.

Not now. This is the most common answer and it is not always a no. Ask two questions: what would need to be true for this to happen, and when can we look at it again. "What would need to be in place for a review in six months?" is a good question, because it turns a refusal into a target. Say thank you, write down what was said, and do the work. Then come back on the date, with new evidence.

No. Do not argue in the room, and do not walk out. Stay calm, ask why, and listen to the reason, because it usually contains information: a budget freeze, a policy that pay rises follow a review cycle, or a belief that you are not yet at the level you are asking for. That last one is painful but useful, because it tells you what to do. Ask: "Is there anything I can do in the next six months that would put this within reach?" Then thank the manager for being honest with you.

If you are disappointed, it is fine to say so, once, without blame: "I am sorry to hear that; I had hoped for a different answer." Then stop. Do not cry, do not sulk, and do not say "I will look for other jobs" in the room, unless you mean it and are ready to be asked to leave immediately.

One thing to avoid in every case: **threatening to leave as a tactic**. If you say "I have an offer elsewhere", be ready to be asked for it, and be ready to go if you say it. Empty threats are remembered, and they cost more than they win.
examples: Thank you, I appreciate that. Can I see the revised figure in writing, and when does it start?
What would need to be in place for a review in six months?
I am sorry to hear that; I had hoped for a different answer.
Is there anything I can do in the next six months that would put this within reach?
sections.heading: How to handle the answer

sections.body:
These are the terms you will hear, and using them correctly makes you sound informed rather than demanding.

A **pay review** or **salary review** is the regular discussion of your pay. A **performance review** is a separate conversation about your work, and it usually happens first. **To be reviewed** means to have your pay looked at again.

A pay band or **salary band** is the range a role is paid within, with a minimum, a midpoint and a maximum. **The midpoint** is the middle of that range. If you are below the midpoint of your band, that is a fact you can put in your case without any emotion at all. **A pay grade** is the same idea at a different level of detail.

Benchmarking means comparing your pay with the market. **A benchmark** is the comparison figure. **To market-adjust** means to move a salary to the market rate. **Cost of living** is the effect of prices and inflation on what you can afford, and **a cost-of-living increase** is a rise meant to match inflation.

Total compensation is everything you receive, not only the salary: bonus, allowances, benefits, insurance. **A bonus** is a payment that depends on results. **A one-off adjustment** is a single increase that does not change your base salary. **A market correction** is usually the same thing, and it is a better term to hear, because it frames the increase as a fix rather than a reward.

A promotion is a change of role and often of band. **A regrade** is a change of level within the same job. **To be made redundant** means to be let go because the role has gone. **Notice period** is the time you must give before leaving. **Severance** is the payment made when a job ends.

And two words for the negotiation itself: **to negotiate** is to discuss the terms, and **negotiating** is not aggressive if you do it calmly. **To counter** an offer means to respond with a different figure, and it is the correct word when the employer says "we can offer $1,650" and you are going to say no.
sections.heading: The words of a pay conversation, one by one

terms.example: My pay review is at the end of March, so I asked to be included.
terms.gloss: A regular discussion of your pay, often once a year, separate from a performance review.

terms.example: I had a strong performance review, and I want to use it in my pay case.
terms.gloss: A formal conversation with your manager about your work and how you are doing, usually held before a pay review.

terms.example: My band goes from $1,400 to $1,900, and I am currently below the midpoint.
terms.gloss: The range a role is paid within, with a minimum, a midpoint and a maximum.

terms.example: I am about $120 below the midpoint for my band.
terms.gloss: The middle figure of a pay band, usually the point where an employee is expected to be fully competent.

terms.example: The benchmark for this role in Hanoi is around $1,750.
terms.gloss: A figure used to compare your pay with the market rate for the same role.

terms.example: My total compensation is $1,650, including the transport allowance.
terms.gloss: Everything you receive from a job: salary, bonus, allowances and benefits, not only the monthly pay.

terms.example: I asked whether a higher bonus could work instead of a permanent increase.
terms.gloss: A payment that depends on results, usually agreed at the start of the year.

terms.example: They offered a one-off adjustment of $150 for this year.
terms.gloss: A single increase to pay that does not change your base salary.

terms.example: The company called it a market correction, which is still a pay rise.
terms.gloss: An increase given to bring pay in line with the market, framed as a fix rather than a reward.

terms.example: They suggested a regrade to senior analyst.
terms.gloss: A change of level within the same job, which usually comes with a pay band change.

terms.example: I can give one month of notice, so I could start in April.
terms.gloss: The amount of time you must give before leaving a job, commonly one or two months.

terms.example: The package included three months of salary as severance.
terms.gloss: A payment made to an employee when a job ends, often calculated by years of service.

terms.example: They offered $1,650, so I countered with $1,800.
terms.gloss: To respond to an offer with a different figure, as in a negotiation.

sections.body:
Comparing yourself to a colleague. "Mai earns more than me and we do the same job" is a complaint about fairness, not a case about value. It also puts you at odds with a colleague you have to work with tomorrow.

Waiting for a perfect moment. There is no perfect moment. Waiting a year because you are still "not ready" is the most common way people lose a year.

Apologising for asking. "I am sorry to ask, and I know you have a lot on" undercuts your case before it starts. You are not asking for a favour.

Naming a figure you cannot justify. If you ask for $2,000 when the band ends at $1,900, the conversation ends on the band, not on your evidence. Ask for a number your case supports.

Threatening to leave. If you say you have an offer, be ready to produce it and be ready to be asked for it. Empty threats are remembered.

Sending the request and nothing else, with no number. An email that says "I would like to discuss my compensation" gives the manager no reason to act, and it will be answered in three weeks by a calendar invitation. Put the number in the email.
sections.heading: Six mistakes that end a pay conversation early

sections.body:
The conversation is not the end of the process. What you do in the following week decides whether this pays off.

Put it in writing. Send a short email the same day or the next morning: thank them, summarise what was agreed in one or two sentences, and attach any revised figures. "Thank you for the conversation today. To confirm, my salary moves to $1,800 per month from 1 April, and the revised contract is attached." If nothing was agreed, write what was said instead: "Thank you for talking it through. As we discussed, we will look at the request again in October, and you asked me to bring cost savings from the reporting work in June." Writing it down prevents a misunderstanding, and it is a normal, professional thing to do.

Do the work you said you would do. If you offered evidence for a review in six months, deliver it early and in writing. This is the single biggest factor in whether you get a yes next time.

Keep your own record. A private note of what you achieved, what you asked for, what you were offered and when you agreed to revisit it. Keep it in a document you control, not in your work email, because the company can change systems and delete files. Personal notes on your own machine are the safer record.

Know when to come back. If you agreed to a review date, put a reminder in your calendar for a week before it and start preparing then, not on the day. If there was no date given, ask for one: "What would be a sensible point to come back to this?"

Have a plan for the next market move. If the answer is a firm no and you have no reason to expect it to change, the question becomes whether to stay or to look. That is a bigger decision than a pay conversation, and it deserves its own preparation rather than being decided in a bad afternoon.

And remember what a no is not. A no is a decision about one number on one day, not a judgement about your worth or your future. Many people get a raise on the second ask, and the second ask usually only happens because the first one was made properly.
examples: To confirm, my salary moves to $1,800 per month from 1 April, and the revised contract is attached.
As we discussed, we will look at the request again in October.
I am documenting this for my own records: what was agreed and when.
What would be a sensible point to come back to this?
sections.heading: What to do after the conversation

item.summary: A request for a raise is a business case, not a favour. It works when you arrive with evidence, a number and a calm plan. After reading this you will know when to ask, how to build the evidence, how to say the sentence out loud, and what to do in the week after you hear no.
item.title: How to Ask for a Raise Politely
